name: Nassella
common_group: Texas needlegrasses — one canonical species plus comparison-only lookalikes

priority: winter-active perennial bunch and dark rough blades
open spring panicle with individual one-flowered spikelets
ONE long twisted, bent awn per mature lemma
elongate needle-sharp often hairy callus on the HARD fruit
pale membranous crown/neck at awn base
1-mm-scale fruit lemma and callus contrast against Mexican feathergrass
study_strategy.warning: One long awn is not unique to Texas wintergrass. Several Nassella have one awn; use mature fruit size and callus shape with attached panicle and leaf characters. Aristida has three awns FROM ONE lemma, not simply three awns visible across a head.
field_sequence: Start with green late-fall-to-early-spring cool-season bunch; photograph rooted plant plus full flowering panicle.
Inspect one fertile individual spikelet in the branching panicle. Glumes may persist after fruit dispersal and look oat-like.
Find ONE rope-twisted and bent lemma awn on each fruit. Compare THREE awn branches off ONE Aristida lemma.
At 10–20× examine needle-sharp lower CALLUS, pale upper corona/crown, and long awn insertion.
If needlegrass, compare N. tenuissima: filamentous blades, lemma ~1.8–3.6 mm, short callus ~0.2–0.4 mm; leucotricha larger lemma ~5.3–13 mm and callus ~1.2–5.5 mm.
Keep uncertain sterile clumps Nassella sp. and schedule fruiting-season photos, do not label native plant an invasive cultivar from overall shape.
study_strategy.taxon_scope: Only N. leucotricha is installed; Mexican feathergrass comparison-only, with distinct Texas ornamental/escaped status not audited or locally certified here.

look_here_first: ONE INSTALLED GENUS MEMBER: Texas wintergrass (Nassella leucotricha). Begin at the winter GREEN bunch (physically photographed), trace the usually open/loosish SPRING flowerhead bearing attached small spikelets on long awns (physically photographed), then select ONE mature floret. In the USDA public-domain fruit image three arrows show the REAL sharply pointed, often hairy CALLUS at its base, the hardened lemma body, and its SINGLE long twice-bent twisted awn. Be careful: THREE awn branches on ONE lemma = Aristida; Mexican feathergrass still has ONE awn but an exceptionally short obtuse callus and much smaller lemma. No precise local crown/ligule macro yet. New photographed teaching stages (Harms) show sheath, attached flowering spikelets, one long bent lemma awn and empty persistent glumes. Preserve distinct source rights; not every panel is the same specimen.

comparison_lesson.title: Texas wintergrass versus THREE-AWN and Mexican feathergrass
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: ONE twisted long awn + SHARP callus (Texas wintergrass); THREE awns from ONE lemma (Aristida); tiny short blunt callus + thread leaves (Mexican feathergrass).
quick_split: N. leucotricha — only Nassella installed in this learner. Look for actively green winter/spring tuft, actual spring panicle, and a single hardened fertile lemma with ONE long bent/twisted awn and an elongated sharply pointed often hairy callus. Kew typically awn 50–60 mm, FNA 40–90 mm, separate reports vary.
Aristida purpurea / A. oligantha — THREE separate awn limbs from each one lemma, not one; oldfield annual and purple perennial, so don't decide only on life cycle.
N. tenuissima — Mexican feathergrass, also SINGLE-awed; finer rolled blades, smaller hard lemma ~1.8–3.6 mm and short obtuse callus ~0.2–0.4 mm compared with Texas wintergrass.
Little bluestem / Schizachyrium scoparium — warm-season with separate short silky racemes on different upper leafy branches, not an open cool-season one-awed panicle.
Canada / Virginia wildrye — cool-season bunches with distinct terminal SPIKES of clusters of spikelets, not Nassella's loose branching panicle.
comparison_lesson.important_caution: The two new CC BY JPEGs show a winter tuft and spring awned head, not a measured mature fruit. A single-awed stalk can also be N. tenuissima, so count awns on ONE intact lemma and measure the size/shape of sharp callus and corona. From FNA N. leucotricha can have 1–5.5 mm sharp callus, crown 0.75–2 mm, membrane ligule 0.2–1.2 mm; herbarium specimen identification still requires more than photography. Never count an image of OTHER species as N. leucotricha or alter native-county claims.
photo_targets: Already installed/arrowed: winter-active basal leafy tuft (John Thomlinson CC BY) and true awned spring flowering head (Sam Kieschnick CC BY); no need to source more identical wide habitat views.
Next one Hays-area attached whole rooted bunch plus spring panicle in single confirmed specimen set, comparable scale.
Next short true MEMBRANOUS ligule with mm scale (FNA typically 0.2–1.2 mm) and leaf collar hairs if present; do not arrow hidden ligule.
Next intact mature sharp hairy CALLUS measuring ~1–5.5 mm and pale corona/crown 0.75–2 mm, photograph from side at 10–20× with mm scale.
Reproductive macro WITH glumes, the hard single-awed fertile lemma and base callus in same traceable specimen.
Matched N. tenuissima much shorter blunt callus and single-awed lemma macro; purple/oldfield Aristida THREE awn branches on one single mature lemma.

visual_comparison.title: Nassella — green bunch → spring panicle → sharp one-awed fruit
visual_comparison.subtitle: 10 photos, including four actual Bob Harms educational-use close-ups with real scale bars: blade/sheath, flowering, hardened one-awed fruit and post-fruit glumes. Original source credit and non-CC limit retained. Four Harms genus panels now reference the same physically stored species images; USDA remains remote.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: N. leucotricha: winter-active bunch, attached loose-to-narrow flowering panicle, mature lemma with ONE long twice-bent rope-twisted AWN and a LONG SHARP HAIRY CALLUS. Aristida has THREE awn branches on ONE lemma; N. tenuissima also ONE awn, but much smaller blunt callus.

items.label: 1 · WINTER TUFT — actual green bunch among dry leaves
items.image_role: Actual archived source-determined Texas wintergrass vegetative tuft; narrow live green blades in dry litter, no seedhead in this photograph
items.caption: True pixel-inspected archived photograph shows multiple fine green blades arising in a dense small bunch amid brown fallen leaves and dry blades. This is HABIT evidence only: there is no exposed root/collar, no confirmed attached panicle, and no flowering character that independently determines the species.
items.why_it_matters: Crew first look in late fall to spring: locate the green cool-season bunch, but wait for mature fruit before naming Texas wintergrass.
items.creator: John Thomlinson
items.photo_status: 2026-10-21 inspected actual 1400x933 JPEG stored in canonical folder, archived GBIF CC BY/John Thomlinson record; original exact photo license version and taxon independently unreviewed, retained provisional. One arrow marks visibly dense green leaf tuft only.

items.label: 2 · SPRING HEAD — source-identified awned panicle in hand
items.image_role: Real photographed Texas wintergrass open-to-narrow panicle with several attached slender sharp-looking spikelets and long awns against a hand
items.caption: Archived Sam Kieschnick photograph visibly shows slender branching panicle with multiple narrow florets and exceptionally long threadlike AWNS, fingers behind for broad size. Photograph is not a dissection and cannot establish actual callus length, lemma corona or glume veins. Do NOT label multiple awn threads in this image as one three-awned Aristida fruit.
items.why_it_matters: Links field recognition of a real awned spring flowering head to the USDA enlarged example showing ONE awn on ONE hardened lemma.
items.creator: Sam Kieschnick
items.photo_status: 2026-10-21 inspected actual 1050x1400 JPEG stored in canonical folder, archived GBIF CC BY/Sam Kieschnick record; source species determination follows recorded observation and original per-photo license version recheck desirable. Two conservative gross structure arrows, no invisible microscopic claims.

items.label: Texas wintergrass — single-awed fruit from Victoria County, Texas
items.image_role: Physically viewed public-domain USDA-ARS original at full 900×600 resolution: one upper sharp white-haired pointed callus, hardened lemma body and its single long twisted awn; three true structure arrows
items.caption: Full 900×600 USDA original photo from Victoria, Texas shows three separate fruit+awn pieces on a purple background. TOP fruit, left to right: sharp white-haired pointed CALLUS; ochre hardened LEMMA/fruit; one extraordinarily long ROPE-TWISTED awn extending right. Three arrows are anchored on those exact visible regions. Other portions of the picture belong to other florets: do not mistake them for three awns from one lemma.
items.why_it_matters: Best verified public reference for the needle-like fruit. It teaches what a one-awned grass floret looks like, unlike the three arms on one Aristida lemma.
items.creator: Tracey Slotta / USDA-ARS
items.photo_status: EXACT photo inspected in full at 900×600 on 2026-10-21 via Wikimedia original (upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/Nassella_leucotricha.jpg). Three gross-structure arrows visually verified; no claim of measured crown/ligule or species ID solely on one detached fruit.

items.label: Texas wintergrass — winter field reference from Abilene
items.image_role: Source-labelled February Texas wintergrass vegetation, useful seasonal vegetative habit reference (nonlocal to Hays)
items.caption: Abilene (Taylor County) observation, February 25, 2025. Shows a living winter-season example of the native grass; species-level callus, awn column and sheath collar are not independently verified within the image. CC BY-NC original photo; public noncommercial project use only.
items.why_it_matters: Demonstrates why a green cool-season bunch can remain active while warm-season prairie grasses are dormant, but is not a stand-alone diagnostic ID.
items.creator: amandagvaughn
items.photo_status: Per-photo iNaturalist license independently verified as CC BY-NC, observation research grade with two source IDs; not physically installed, do not make precise anatomical arrows.

items.label: Purple threeawn — three bristles arise from each lemma
items.image_role: Already installed, credited purple-threeawn floret/awn photograph; genus contrast, not Nassella photo
items.caption: PURPLE THREEAWN COMPARISON: typically three spreading branches arise from ONE lemma; Texas wintergrass has only ONE long awn on a floret. Count on the same mature lemma—not from a whole panicle.
items.why_it_matters: Prevents mistaking three awns on an Aristida floret for three different one-awned florets.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Existing real archived purple-threeawn macro, source labelled; no new arrow placed from this reused photo.

items.label: Mexican feathergrass — look-alike ONE-awed plant (comparison only)
items.image_role: CC BY-SA 3.0 cultivated ornamental Mexican feathergrass habit photographed Las Vegas, comparison-only
items.caption: Mexican feathergrass is also a SINGLE-awed Nassella. Its very narrow threadlike rolled leaves and much smaller fruit/callus distinguish it from Texas wintergrass; vegetation-only photographs are supporting evidence, not a glume/lemma macro.
items.why_it_matters: Shows why 'only one awn' establishes a needlegrass-type candidate but is not unique to Texas wintergrass.
items.creator: Stan Shebs
items.photo_status: Wikimedia source rights and cultivated Las Vegas origin verified; comparison-only species, no made-up fruit arrows.

items.why_it_matters: Provides real leaf/scaly sheath structure and clarifies that the ~0.5mm ligule still needs a closer photo.
